question.text: Mr. Ramesh Iyer, proposed CIO of 'Saraswati Opportunities Fund', is finalising the Trust Deed and LLP-Manager structure. Under SEBI (AIF) Regulations, 2012, which of the following is an accurate statement on the compulsory registration requirement for all AIFs domiciled in India?

answer.text: Only close-ended AIFs with corpus exceeding INR 100 crore are required to register; smaller funds may operate as unregistered pools.
AIFs domiciled in IFSC/GIFT City are exempt from SEBI registration and are regulated solely by IFSCA with no SEBI oversight.
An AIF can commence investment activities immediately on filing Form A; registration with SEBI can be completed within 24 months from first close.

All existing and proposed AIFs domiciled in India are subject to compulsory registration with SEBI; existing schemes may complete their agreed tenure but cannot raise fresh monies beyond commitments already made until registration is granted.

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook states that all existing and proposed AIFs domiciled in India must compulsorily register with SEBI, and that existing schemes are not permitted to raise fresh monies until registration is granted, although they may continue to complete their agreed tenure. After in-principle approval, an AIF may accept commitments but cannot accept money before grant of the registration certificate. The Trap: Option A invents a corpus-based threshold for registration, which the workbook does not support. Option B overstates the IFSC carve-out; AIFs in IFSC are still within SEBI's regulatory perimeter. Option C is the premature-commencement claim, allowing investments before registration and giving a 24-month grace period, neither of which is supported by the workbook. Note: Registration is universal for India-domiciled AIFs. Between Form A and grant of the certificate, only commitments (post in-principle approval) may be accepted; fresh monies cannot be drawn until the registration certificate is issued.
